RB-16 · Under the hood

No samples. Every drum is math.

The RB-16 doesn't load a single audio file. Each kick, snare and hat is built in real time from oscillators and filtered noise through the Web Audio API, then scheduled against the audio clock so the groove never drifts. Here's how.

1 · Synthesizing the voices

A classic analog drum machine doesn't play recordings — it generates each sound electronically. We do the same in JavaScript. Every voice is a tiny graph of OscillatorNodes, a BufferSource of noise, biquad filters and a gain envelope, assembled the instant a hit fires and torn down when it finishes.

VoiceBuilt fromKnobs change…
KickA sine pitch-swept from ~150 Hz down to ~45 Hz, plus an optional triangle "click" transient.Tune sets start/end pitch, Decay the body length, Tone the click punch.
SnareA pair of detuned triangles for the body, mixed with high-passed + band-passed noise for the rattle.Tone balances body vs. noise; Tune shifts both up or down.
ClapBand-passed noise re-triggered three times ~12 ms apart, then a diffuse tail — the trick that makes a clap sound like many hands.Decay stretches the tail, Tune moves the bandpass.
Hats & CrashSix (or eight) square oscillators at inharmonic ratios through a bandpass + highpass — the metallic, pitchless shimmer.Decay is open vs. closed; Tone the brightness.
TomsA falling sine with a short noise attack.Tune picks the drum size; Decay the sustain.
Cowbell / RimTwo detuned squares through a sharp bandpass (cowbell) or two fast square blips (rim).Tune the pitch, Decay the ring.

Because nothing is pre-recorded, a "kit" is just a table of numbers. Loading the 808 kit instead of the 909 only changes those numbers — the synthesis code is identical, the result is a totally different machine.

2 · The lookahead scheduler

The hard part of any sequencer isn't making sound — it's making sound on time. A naïve setInterval that fires a drum every beat will stutter the moment the browser is busy laying out the page or running garbage collection. setTimeout and requestAnimationFrame are simply not accurate enough for music.

So the RB-16 uses the pattern Chris Wilson described in "A Tale of Two Clocks": a coarse JavaScript timer that only ever schedules ahead, and the rock-solid audio clock (AudioContext.currentTime) that decides when notes actually play.

// a 25 ms timer just looks ahead ~100 ms and enqueues notes
setInterval(function () {
  while (nextNoteTime < ctx.currentTime + SCHEDULE_AHEAD) {
    scheduleStep(step, nextNoteTime);   // fire drums AT nextNoteTime
    nextNoteTime += secondsPerStep();   // advance the musical clock
    step = (step + 1) % steps;
  }
}, 25);

Every drum is started with an exact timestamp — osc.start(nextNoteTime) — so even if the JavaScript timer wakes up a few milliseconds late, the audio still plays sample-accurately. The grid highlight is the only thing driven by wall-clock time, queued and flushed as each step's moment arrives, so the visuals can be loose while the sound stays tight.

JS timer · 25 ms
looks ahead → enqueues at exact times →
Audio clock · sample-accurate

3 · Swing, accents & song mode

Swing simply delays every odd 16th-note by a fraction of a step, pushing the off-beats late for that human, behind-the-beat shuffle. Accents and ghost notes are per-step velocities (1.2 / 0.55) that scale each hit's gain — shift-click a cell to cycle them. Song mode chains pattern banks A–D into a track: when a pattern finishes its repeats, the scheduler swaps in the next bank's grid between bars, so the chain plays seamlessly.

4 · The mix bus

Every voice runs through its own track gain (for level, mute and solo), summed into a bus, gently soft-clipped by a WaveShaper "drive", then through a DynamicsCompressor acting as a limiter so a busy beat or a panic stab never clips your speakers. An AnalyserNode taps the master output to feed the canvas visualizer.

voices→ track gain
level · mute · solo→ bus→ drive
soft clip→ master→ limiter→ analyser→ speakers

5 · Specs & accessibility

  • Engine — Web Audio API. No samples, no libraries, no build step. Open index.html over file:// and it runs.
  • Voices — 10 synthesized drums; each with Tune / Decay / Tone / Level.
  • Sequencer — 16 steps, adjustable 4–16 steps per bar, 40–240 BPM, swing to 60%, per-step accents & ghosts.
  • Arranger — 4 pattern banks + a chain-based song mode.
  • Persistence — kits & beats saved to localStorage; export / import a song as JSON.
  • Accessibility — fully keyboard-operable, ARIA-labelled controls, and the visualizer calms its motion under prefers-reduced-motion.
  • Audio policy — the AudioContext is created on your first click, per the browser autoplay rules; if Web Audio is unavailable the UI degrades gracefully.

The makers

Pulseforge is a two-person studio that builds playable instruments for the open web — no plugins, no downloads, no accounts. The RB-16 is our love letter to the rhythm boxes that shaped a half-century of music.
